chapter: Black writers, Harvard and Down Beat
title: Writing peers: Martin Williams, Whitney Balliett and others
summary: He admired Williams and Balliett and recalls the camaraderie with Hsio Wen Shih, Stearns and Dan Morgenstern.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Let’s talk about your peers as a writer in the early 1950s. Was there a sense of community with – eventually, when people came to New York, like Martin Williams and/or the others – Whitney Balliett, these people who you had historic collaborations with?

Yeah. Once I read Martin, I knew I was in the presence of somebody I had to learn from. Same thing with Whitney: nobody was ever able to put the music into words without being precious or self-exalted, etc., and he also had very good ears. I liked him. He was – both – Martin, and there was a guy named Hsio Wen Shih who wrote very well historically. Yeah, there was some camaraderie. Marshall Stearns was part of that scene, come to think of it. Eventually Dan Morgenstern and all that. Yeah, there was a lot of that.
So you’re saying that it’s the Village Voice column is when you began to expand your written topics outside of just jazz music.
